Sources of social change: technology, ideas, conflict, and the environment (one line plus an original example each)
Slow vs sudden change: gradual drift vs rapid rupture

Unintended consequences of change (Ogburn's cultural lag)

claims.claim: Social change is the alteration of social structures, institutions, and patterns of interaction over time; OpenStax's Introduction to Sociology 3e (21.3) describes it as the change in society — essentially any disruptive shift in the status quo, be it intentional or random, human-caused or natural.

Technology is a recurring source of social change: new tools and techniques reshape daily life and alter the other forces of society (medical technology extends lives; agricultural technology alters food; communication technology rearranges work and community life).

Ideas can drive social change: Max Weber argued that the West was characterized by a peculiar type of rationality that had brought about modern capitalism, modern science, and rational law — distinctive ways of thinking reordering institutions.

Conflict between groups with opposed interests drives social change: in Karl Marx's account, social development is a dialectical process in which the transition from one stage to another takes place through revolutionary transformation preceded by intensified class struggle.

The environment is a source of social change: natural forces and disasters reshape societies, and their effects typically combine with other factors (OpenStax's Hurricane Katrina discussion shows environment, technology, population, and institutions converging).

Social change varies in tempo: some change is gradual and cumulative (Spencer's evolutionary development; Marx's gradual development of the forces of production), while some arrives as a sudden rupture (a revolutionary transformation; any disruptive shift in the status quo).

Evolutionary theory of social change (19th century, associated with Herbert Spencer): as societies grow in size they become more complex; their parts differentiate, specialize, and become more interdependent. This line of thought has since been disputed and disproved.
Conflict theory of social change (associated with Karl Marx): societies change through tension between groups with opposed interests, and major transformations follow intensified struggle.

Change brings unintended consequences: William F. Ogburn (1922) defined cultural lag, which occurs when material culture precedes nonmaterial culture — society may not fully comprehend all the consequences of a new technology and may embrace it, sometimes with unintended negative consequences (such as pollution).

Change is not the same as progress: in neoevolutionist thought, evolutionary development is not equated with progress, and OpenStax 3e 21.3 asks whether modernization is always positive, noting that time-saving technologies have not reduced average housework time and that ethnocentric bias marks modernization assessments.

OpenStax 3e 21.3 organizes the causes of social change as four agents — technology, social institutions, population, and the environment — working alone or in combination, and notes that each change in a single social institution leads to changes in all social institutions.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Different texts carve the list of causes of social change differently. OpenStax 3e 21.3 names four agents: technology, social institutions, population, and the environment. This lesson's topic brief requires the four sources technology, ideas, conflict, and environment.
positions: OpenStax 3e 21.3: technology, social institutions, population, environment

Topic brief (this lesson): technology, ideas, conflict, environment — ideas supported by Weber's rationality argument and conflict by Marx's class-struggle account, both per Britannica's 'Social change' article
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the brief's four sources (technology, ideas, conflict, environment), names OpenStax's four agents in one sentence so the textbook's framing is not misrepresented, and notes that the lists overlap — technology and environment appear in both.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether change is progressive. Nineteenth-century evolutionism equated development with progress; later theorists rejected that equation.
positions: Classical evolutionism (Spencer): societies develop along a line of predetermined, inevitable progress
Later sociology (neoevolutionism; OpenStax's modernization critique): evolutionary development is not equated with progress; modernization is not automatically positive
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the honest note that change is not the same as progress, citing both Britannica (neoevolutionism) and OpenStax 3e 21.3 (modernization critique), with no position on whether any particular change is good or bad.

sourceRecords.title: 21.3 Social Change — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. New id minted — no existing registry record for any section-21 URL of this book. Read live via direct HTTP fetch (curl with a browser user-agent) of the canonical 3e page on 2026-08-22. Supports: the working definition of social change as the change in society — any disruptive shift in the status quo, intentional or random, human-caused or natural; the four agents of change (technology, social institutions, population, environment) working alone or in combination; technology's effects on daily life and other social forces; the interconnection of social institutions; population change as a driver; the environment as a driver (including the Hurricane Katrina convergence discussion); Ogburn's (1922) cultural lag and unintended consequences (e.g., pollution); the modernization definition (Irwin 1975) and the critique that modernization is not always positive (housework-time paradox, ethnocentric bias). Facts synthesized in original wording; one short phrase quoted with attribution. Note: openstax.org now serves near-identical content on the 2e section URL as well; the 3e canonical URL was used.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. The live britannica.com page is Cloudflare-blocked to curl; read via Internet Archive captures of the canonical URL (2025 and 2023 timestamps; both read 2026-08-22). Supports: the three basic ideas of social change (decline, cyclic change, continuous progress); 19th-century evolutionism and Herbert Spencer's evolutionary law (a change from relative homogeneity to definite, coherent heterogeneity — societies grow in size, become more complex, and their parts differentiate, specialize, and become more interdependent) and the later verdict that this line of thought has been disputed and disproved; Marx's dialectical account (revolutionary transformation preceded by intensified class struggle; the combination of dialectics and gradualism); Weber's claim that a peculiar type of rationality brought about modern capitalism, modern science, and rational law in the West; the neoevolutionist point that evolutionary development is not equated with progress; modernization-theory critiques (Western-centred assumptions). Facts synthesized in original wording; no source prose adapted.
